title: A Comprehensive Review of Autophagy and Its Various Roles in Infectious, Non-Infectious, and Lifestyle Diseases: Current Knowledge and Prospects for Disease Prevention, Novel Drug Design, and Therapy

subsections.section_title: Molecular Foundations and Regulatory Architecture of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Molecular Foundations and Regulatory Architecture of Autophagy - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Autophagy is a conserved lysosome-directed quality-control pathway that enables cells to recycle proteins, lipids, and organelles in response to nutrient limitation, energetic stress, and damage. As a foundational homeostatic process, it links biosynthetic economy with stress adaptation and helps determine whether cells maintain viability or transition toward dysfunction. This duality is particularly evident in settings of tumorigenesis, metabolic remodeling, and organ-specific adaptation, where autophagy can either buffer stress or support disease persistence depending on context ref [2], ref [11], ref [12].

At the regulatory level, autophagy is tightly coupled to cellular energy sensing. AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) functions as a central node that responds to falling ATP availability and promotes survival programs, including autophagic flux, whereas nutrient-replete states generally suppress this catabolic response ref [4], ref [11], ref [12]. Beyond bulk turnover, autophagy also participates in selective metabolic remodeling; autophagic lipolysis mobilizes lipid droplets to sustain energy balance, illustrating how the pathway is integrated into systemic and intracellular fuel management ref [5], ref [12]. These principles are especially relevant in metabolically demanding tissues such as the heart, where autophagy supports cardiomyocyte adaptation to altered substrate use and ischemic stress ref [4], ref [11].

Autophagy is further embedded in broader cellular surveillance networks. Its crosstalk with ubiquitination helps specify cargo recognition and coordinates proteostatic responses with genome maintenance pathways, including DNA repair-associated stress responses ref [9]. Mitochondrial dysfunction can also intersect with autophagy-driven inflammatory control, highlighting how defective organelle handling contributes to autoinflammatory signaling ref [18]. Finally, the endpoint of autophagic degradation depends on lysosomal competence; disruption of lysosomal function compromises flux and underlies several storage disorders, emphasizing that autophagy should be understood as an integrated pathway rather than only vesicle formation ref [21], ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Molecular Foundations and Regulatory Architecture of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Molecular Foundations and Regulatory Architecture of Autophagy - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Autophagy is also shaped by neuromodulatory and lipid-signaling systems that influence cellular stress adaptation, membrane dynamics, and metabolic homeostasis. In this broader regulatory context, the endocannabinoid system has emerged as a relevant upstream modulator because cannabinoid receptors engage G-protein-dependent and -independent signaling cascades that intersect with kinase networks, calcium fluxes, cAMP signaling, and survival pathways known to affect autophagic responses ref [10], ref [16], ref [19]. The expanding pharmacological landscape of cannabis-derived compounds has therefore stimulated interest in how receptor bias, ligand selectivity, and non-canonical targets may differentially tune stress-responsive programs, including autophagy-related outputs ref [10], ref [12], ref [16].

Mechanistically, CB1 and CB2 receptor signaling is not uniform: biased agonism and context-dependent coupling can generate divergent downstream effects, implying that autophagy regulation by cannabinoids is likely cell-type specific rather than universally activating or suppressive ref [10], ref [19]. This complexity is further reinforced by non-CB1/non-CB2 GPCRs and other cannabinoid-responsive targets, which broaden the regulatory architecture through additional layers of intracellular signaling integration ref [19]. Experimental and translational work in the 2010s highlighted this heterogeneity, showing that cannabinoid biology cannot be reduced to a single pathway and that formulation, exposure route, and pharmacokinetics may substantially alter biological outcomes relevant to membrane trafficking and stress handling ref [9], ref [12], ref [16].

From a disease-oriented perspective, these regulatory nuances are important because chronic or developmental cannabinoid exposure can reshape neuronal and systemic physiology, potentially modifying basal proteostatic and metabolic set points that intersect with autophagy-dependent homeostasis ref [11], ref [20]. Clinical and user-reported studies likewise indicate substantial variability in duration, dose, perceived efficacy, and symptom domains targeted by cannabis or cannabidiol-based interventions, emphasizing that any putative autophagy-directed therapeutic exploitation will require rigorous standardization and mechanism-aware trial design ref [13], ref [15], ref [18]. Related discussions in research and educational initiatives have underscored the need for better biopharmaceutical characterization and translational frameworks before cannabinoid-linked modulation of core homeostatic pathways, including autophagy, can be rationally leveraged in prevention or therapy ref [12], ref [14], ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Molecular Foundations and Regulatory Architecture of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Molecular Foundations and Regulatory Architecture of Autophagy - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Autophagy is tightly integrated with broader stress-signaling and membrane-regulatory systems, and this integration is especially evident in studies of cannabinoid biology. Reviews of cannabis pharmacology show that cannabinoid ligands engage pleiotropic receptor networks with consequences for intracellular calcium handling, kinase activation, mitochondrial function, and cell-survival programs, all of which are upstream determinants of autophagic flux ref [21], ref [30]. Structural analyses of CB1 allosteric modulation further indicate that receptor conformation can bias downstream signaling strength and pathway selection, providing a useful conceptual framework for how extracellular cues may tune autophagy indirectly through GPCR-dependent signaling architecture ref [22].

This signaling plasticity has pathophysiological implications across neurological, infectious, and malignant contexts. Heavy cannabis exposure has been associated with altered executive function, psychomotor performance, and hippocampal structure, with moderation by aerobic fitness and by DAT1, COMT, and BDNF polymorphisms, suggesting that autophagy-relevant stress adaptation is embedded within gene-environment interactions rather than governed by a single linear pathway ref [23], ref [24]. In malaria-infected hosts, oral Cannabis sativa exposure has been discussed in relation to immunological and systemic effects that could intersect with host stress responses ref [25]. In oncology, cannabinoid-based symptom management and ligand-protein interaction mapping in neuroblastoma cells underscore the translational importance of understanding how receptor-proximal signaling interfaces with proteostasis and survival machinery, including autophagy-linked nodes ref [26], ref [32].

At the systems level, these observations emphasize that autophagic regulation is highly context dependent and can be modified by dose, ligand composition, receptor microenvironment, and comorbidity. Clinical and observational reports on psychiatric outcomes, hospitalization in sickle cell disease, and forensic identification of synthetic cannabinoid isomers collectively reinforce that biologically distinct cannabinoid exposures should not be treated as mechanistically equivalent when inferring effects on cellular homeostasis ref [27], ref [28], ref [29], ref [31]. Thus, for autophagy-centered disease models and therapeutic design, a key principle is signaling specificity: small differences at the receptor and ligand level may propagate into substantial differences in stress adaptation, inflammatory balance, and cell fate.

subsections.section_title: Molecular Foundations and Regulatory Architecture of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Molecular Foundations and Regulatory Architecture of Autophagy - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Autophagy is increasingly recognized as a stress-integration hub that interfaces with neuromodulatory and immunometabolic signals, including those triggered by cannabinoids. Title-level evidence from cannabinoid receptor ligand reviews indicates that CB1/CB2 signaling is mechanistically diverse, extending beyond classical neurotransmission to broad regulation of intracellular survival pathways and membrane-associated signaling platforms ref [36], ref [40]. This conceptual breadth is reinforced by work on cannabidiol, which emphasizes pleiotropic pharmacology and supports the view that cannabinoid cues can converge on cellular programs relevant to autophagic adaptation under stress ref [35].

A particularly relevant intersection concerns immune regulation and cell fate. Cannabinoid-induced apoptosis in immune cells has been described as a pathway to immunosuppression, implying functional overlap between cannabinoid-responsive signaling, organelle stress, and downstream degradative or death-associated programs ref [38]. More broadly, research-priority analyses on novel psychoactive substances highlight the need to resolve shared mechanisms of toxicity, adaptation, and homeostatic remodeling at the subcellular level, an agenda that is highly compatible with autophagy-centered models of stress buffering and maladaptation ref [37].

Systems-level observations further suggest that behavioral and physiological stressors linked to cannabinoid exposure may be relevant to autophagy-regulated homeostasis. Studies of cannabis withdrawal during sustained abstinence and of THC effects on sleep architecture indicate persistent perturbations in sleep, arousal, and recovery physiology ref [33], ref [39]. Reviews connecting sleep, pain, and cannabis, together with broader discussions urging investigators to think beyond THC alone, underscore that complex cannabinoid milieus may influence metabolic and inflammatory tone in ways likely to intersect with autophagic control networks ref [34], ref [40]. Although these sources do not directly define core autophagy machinery, they help frame how extracellular cannabinoid signaling can modulate the cellular stress context in which autophagy is activated, restrained, or functionally repurposed ref [35], ref [36].

subsections.section_title: Molecular Foundations and Regulatory Architecture of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Molecular Foundations and Regulatory Architecture of Autophagy - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A further regulatory layer relevant to autophagy is its intersection with the endocannabinoid system, a lipid-signaling network centered on endogenous ligands, cannabinoid receptors, and biosynthetic/degradative enzymes that broadly coordinates energy balance, stress adaptation, and membrane-associated signaling ref [41], ref [50]. From a mechanistic standpoint, this system is pertinent because autophagy is highly sensitive to nutrient cues, intracellular lipid flux, and GPCR-driven second messenger pathways, all of which can be influenced by cannabinoid signaling ref [44], ref [50]. The complexity of this interface is increased by evidence for receptor heterogeneity beyond canonical CB1 and CB2, suggesting that autophagy-relevant outcomes may depend on cell type, receptor context, and ligand bias rather than a single uniform pathway ref [44], ref [49].

This integrative framework is especially important in barrier and metabolic tissues. In the gastrointestinal tract, endocannabinoids participate in epithelial homeostasis, immune regulation, motility, and host–microbe interactions, processes that are also tightly linked to autophagic quality control and inflammatory restraint ref [45], ref [50]. Nutritional cannabinoid-related inputs may further shape this landscape; hempseed contains bioactive lipids and nutraceutical constituents that could, at least conceptually, affect cellular metabolic tone and membrane lipid availability relevant to autophagic regulation ref [47]. These observations support the view that cannabinoid–autophagy crosstalk may become particularly significant in disorders where metabolism, inflammation, and mucosal integrity converge.

Translationally, cannabinoid-based medicines are being actively developed, but their incorporation into autophagy-oriented therapeutic strategies requires careful attention to formulation, route of administration, receptor selectivity, and regulatory context ref [42], ref [48], ref [12]. Distinct cannabinoids can engage different receptors and produce divergent anti-inflammatory or tissue-protective effects, underscoring the need for mechanistically precise pharmacology when considering downstream autophagic consequences ref [49], ref [42]. Clinical and public-health considerations, including use disorders and behavioral effects such as cue reactivity in tobacco withdrawal, further emphasize that systemic cannabinoid interventions may have broader neurobehavioral and safety implications beyond cellular stress signaling ref [46], ref [43]. Accordingly, the cannabinoid system should be regarded as a promising but context-dependent modulator within the wider regulatory architecture of autophagy.

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases and Host-Pathogen Interactions
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases and Host-Pathogen Interactions - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Autophagy is a central component of host defense in infectious disease, coupling intracellular quality control to antimicrobial immunity. In the context of HIV infection, this relationship is notably cell-type specific: macrophages use autophagic machinery as part of innate restriction and inflammatory control, whereas HIV-1 can remodel these pathways to preserve intracellular survival and productive infection ref [20]. In the central nervous system, autophagy is further intertwined with viral life cycle events, innate immune sensing, neuroinflammation, and the persistence of infected myeloid reservoirs, highlighting how a normally protective pathway can become dysregulated during chronic infection ref [52].

The HIV literature also illustrates a broader principle in host-pathogen interactions: pathogens rarely confront autophagy passively. Instead, they suppress autophagosome maturation, redirect membrane trafficking, or exploit selective cargo handling to avoid lysosomal destruction while maintaining access to host nutrients and biosynthetic intermediates ref [52], ref [20]. This duality is especially important in long-lived cells such as macrophages and microglia, where incomplete or altered autophagy may simultaneously favor pathogen persistence and sustain pathological immune activation ref [52], ref [20].

A complementary paradigm is provided by Francisella tularensis, which links intracellular survival to metabolic parasitism. Studies on its “nutritional virulence” show that the pathogen depends on host-derived metabolites and can benefit from host catabolic pathways, including autophagy-related nutrient mobilization, to support replication in nutrient-limited intracellular niches ref [24]. Consistently, targeting bacterial nutrient retrieval has emerged as a therapeutic concept, suggesting that manipulation of host-pathogen metabolic coupling may constrain infection even when pathogens evade canonical microbicidal autophagy ref [22]. Together, HIV and Francisella emphasize that autophagy in infection is not merely degradative; it is also an immunometabolic battleground with direct relevance for host-directed antimicrobial therapy ref [52], ref [20], ref [22], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases and Host-Pathogen Interactions
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases and Host-Pathogen Interactions - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Autophagy contributes to antimicrobial defense by linking cell-intrinsic pathogen restriction with inflammatory signaling and antigen handling. Through selective sequestration of invading microbes or damaged pathogen-containing compartments, autophagy can promote lysosomal destruction, limit intracellular replication, and shape cytokine output. In parallel, autophagic flux influences the quality of antigen presentation and thereby helps connect innate sensing to adaptive immunity, making it a central determinant of host–pathogen balance.

At the same time, many pathogens exploit this pathway rather than simply succumb to it. Some block autophagosome maturation to avoid lysosomal killing, whereas others redirect autophagic membranes and nutrient-recycling functions to create replication-permissive niches. More broadly, host metabolic and immunomodulatory states can alter autophagic competence and thereby reshape susceptibility to infection. This point is conceptually reinforced by literature on cannabinoid signaling and pharmacology, which highlights how receptor-biased signaling, non-canonical cannabinoid-responsive GPCRs, and diverse cannabis-derived formulations can modify immune and inflammatory programs that intersect with autophagy-related pathways ref [10], ref [12], ref [16], ref [20].

These interactions have translational implications. Population and clinical studies of cannabinoid exposure document heterogeneous patterns of use, formulation-dependent effects, and context-specific physiological outcomes, underscoring that host-directed modulation of autophagy or immunity is unlikely to be uniform across individuals ref [9], ref [13], ref [15], ref [12]. Reviews addressing adolescent exposure, broader cannabis research trends, and emerging therapeutic development further emphasize that immunological consequences of such interventions require careful interpretation before extrapolation to infectious-disease settings ref [11], ref [12], ref [14], ref [16], ref [19]. Accordingly, therapeutic strategies targeting autophagy in infection must account not only for pathogen evasion mechanisms but also for host factors and co-exposures that may recalibrate autophagic and immune responses.

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases and Host-Pathogen Interactions
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases and Host-Pathogen Interactions - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
In parasitic infection, autophagy intersects with host metabolism, inflammatory signaling, and xenobiotic exposure, making malaria a useful context for examining how host-directed factors may reshape antimicrobial defense. Although the available evidence is limited, oral Cannabis sativa intake has been discussed in relation to malaria-infected hosts, with emphasis on systemic immunomodulatory and physiological effects that could alter host resilience during infection rather than acting as a direct antiparasitic strategy ref [25]. In this setting, any agent capable of modifying cellular stress responses, nutrient sensing, or inflammatory tone could in principle influence autophagic flux, which is itself tightly linked to immune adaptation and pathogen control ref [25].

This issue is especially relevant because cannabinoid-associated immunosuppression has been described as a consequence of apoptosis and functional attenuation in immune cells, raising the possibility that excessive cannabinoid exposure might weaken autophagy-supported antimicrobial functions in macrophages and other innate immune populations ref [38]. More broadly, the endocannabinoid system regulates inflammatory and metabolic pathways through CB1/CB2-dependent and noncanonical signaling networks, mechanisms that may secondarily converge on autophagy-controlling nodes such as energy sensing, lysosomal function, and stress adaptation ref [42], ref [43], ref [35]. Such crosstalk is biologically plausible in infection, where host cells must balance pathogen restriction against tissue damage.

Accordingly, the relevance of autophagy to host-pathogen interactions in malaria and related infectious states may extend beyond classical xenophagy to include modulation by dietary, phytochemical, and neuroimmune factors. The current literature does not justify therapeutic cannabis use as an anti-infective intervention; instead, it suggests caution, because host-directed exposures that perturb immune homeostasis could either blunt protective autophagic responses or exacerbate disease-associated metabolic stress ref [25], ref [38]. Future work should therefore define whether cannabinoids influence autophagy in infected hepatocytes, erythrocyte-supporting niches, or myeloid cells, and whether these effects are protective, neutral, or permissive for pathogen persistence.

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases and Host-Pathogen Interactions
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases and Host-Pathogen Interactions - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
An important host–pathogen interface in infectious disease is the intersection between autophagy and immunomodulatory pathways that alter leukocyte survival. Cannabinoid signaling is relevant in this context because it can suppress immune competence by inducing apoptosis in immune cells, thereby potentially reshaping the cellular machinery required for xenophagy, cytokine production, and antigen handling. In particular, cannabinoid-induced immune-cell apoptosis has been described as a pathway to immunosuppression, implying that excessive or context-inappropriate activation of this axis could weaken autophagy-assisted antimicrobial defense and favor pathogen persistence ref [6].

This immunosuppressive framework is especially pertinent to infections in which macrophages, dendritic cells, and lymphocytes rely on intact stress-response programs to contain intracellular microbes. Because autophagy supports pathogen sequestration, lysosomal degradation, inflammatory calibration, and crosstalk with adaptive immunity, any exposure that reduces the viability or functional competence of these cells may indirectly compromise host resistance. Thus, even when cannabinoids are discussed primarily in anti-inflammatory or cytoprotective terms, their pro-apoptotic effects in immune populations warrant caution in infectious settings, where attenuation of autophagy-linked immune surveillance could be maladaptive ref [6].

From a translational standpoint, this interaction argues for a context-dependent view of autophagy-targeted therapy during infection. Agents or exposures that alter cannabinoid-responsive immune pathways may have divergent consequences depending on pathogen burden, tissue compartment, and host immune status. Consequently, therapeutic strategies should distinguish between beneficial dampening of damaging inflammation and harmful suppression of autophagy-competent antimicrobial immunity, particularly in patients at risk for chronic, opportunistic, or intracellular infections ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases and Host-Pathogen Interactions
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases and Host-Pathogen Interactions - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A translational perspective on autophagy in infectious disease must also account for host lipid signaling networks, particularly the endocannabinoid system, because these pathways shape inflammation, barrier function, and cellular stress responses that intersect with autophagic control. Broad overviews of the endogenous cannabinoid system and cannabinoid-based therapeutics indicate that CB1/CB2 signaling, endocannabinoid tone, and related lipid mediators regulate immune activation and tissue homeostasis, thereby potentially modifying autophagy-dependent antimicrobial defenses ref [41], ref [47], ref [56], ref [12]. This interface is especially relevant at mucosal surfaces, where endocannabinoids influence epithelial integrity, microbiota-host communication, and intestinal inflammatory tone ref [50].

Although direct infection-focused evidence is limited in the present reference set, available studies support the idea that cannabinoid signaling can reshape host responses in ways likely to affect pathogen handling. Distinct cannabinoid ligands suppress inflammatory pain and local inflammation through different receptor pathways ref [42], while formulation, route of administration, and exposure pattern are recognized determinants of systemic cannabinoid effects ref [46], ref [44]. Nutritional cannabis-derived products such as hempseed further illustrate that bioactive lipid composition can influence baseline metabolic and inflammatory states relevant to autophagy regulation ref [48]. Conversely, behavioral and neuroimmune consequences of prolonged cannabinoid exposure, including persistent dysfunction after adolescent THC treatment and partial protection by cannabidiol, caution that therapeutic manipulation of this axis may have context-dependent costs ref [49].

These considerations have practical implications for host-pathogen interaction research. Cannabidiol and related agents are being advanced as prescription medicines with anti-inflammatory potential ref [47], and human experimental data show measurable central effects of cannabidiol on cue reactivity and behavior ref [51]. For infectious diseases, this argues for careful evaluation of whether cannabinoid-driven dampening of inflammation preserves protective xenophagy and antigen handling or instead creates permissive niches for intracellular microbes. Future work should therefore integrate autophagy biomarkers, pathogen burden, tissue-specific endocannabinoid signaling, and regulatory constraints surrounding cannabidiol deployment ref [44], while leveraging foundational knowledge of the endogenous cannabinoid network to design host-directed therapies that reduce immunopathology without compromising antimicrobial defense ref [41], ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Cancer, Genomic Stability, and Therapeutic Resistance
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Cancer, Genomic Stability, and Therapeutic Resistance - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Autophagy has a fundamentally bidirectional role in cancer biology, acting as a barrier to tumor initiation while also supporting survival of established malignancies under metabolic and therapeutic stress. As summarized in ref [4], basal autophagy limits the accumulation of damaged proteins and organelles, restrains oxidative stress, and helps preserve bioenergetic homeostasis, thereby reducing conditions that favor malignant transformation. However, once tumors are formed, the same recycling machinery can sustain growth in nutrient-poor and hypoxic microenvironments by supplying metabolic substrates and maintaining mitochondrial function, making autophagy highly context dependent in oncology.

A major tumor-suppressive dimension of autophagy lies in the maintenance of genomic integrity. The functional interplay among autophagy, ubiquitination, and DNA repair indicates that autophagic flux contributes indirectly and directly to genome surveillance by clearing damaged cellular components, modulating protein quality control, and intersecting with DNA damage response pathways ref [9]. When this network is impaired, persistent oxidative damage, proteotoxic stress, and defective turnover of repair-related factors can promote chromosomal instability and mutagenic evolution, thereby linking autophagy deficiency to early carcinogenesis ref [9], ref [4].

This duality is especially relevant in oncogene-driven tumors. KRAS-mediated cancers develop within inflammatory and metabolically harsh niches, and inflammatory signaling can both drive tumor progression and create liabilities that intersect with autophagy dependence ref [14]. In such settings, autophagy may buffer oncogenic stress and support tumor cell fitness, suggesting that its inhibition could be advantageous in selected molecular contexts, whereas autophagy preservation may be protective in premalignant states ref [14], ref [4]. Notably, interest in adjunctive anticancer strategies has also extended to cannabinoids, partly because cannabinoid-responsive pathways can influence autophagy and tumor cell fate, although current evidence remains more mechanistic than clinically definitive ref [57].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Cancer, Genomic Stability, and Therapeutic Resistance
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Cancer, Genomic Stability, and Therapeutic Resistance - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
An emerging translational theme in cancer biology is whether cannabinoid-based interventions modulate autophagy in ways that alter tumor survival or treatment response. Although the candidate literature here is primarily preclinical and not centered on autophagy as a sole endpoint, it consistently shows that cannabinoids can trigger stress programs linked to growth arrest and cell death in breast and colorectal cancer models, thereby positioning autophagy as a plausible component of the broader cytotoxic response rather than an isolated mechanism ref [9], ref [21], ref [42].

In breast cancer models, comparison of a purified cannabinoid with a botanical preparation challenged simplistic assumptions about the “entourage effect,” showing that antitumor efficacy depends on composition, dose, and cellular context ref [9]. In colorectal systems, both combinations of cannabis-derived compounds and synthetic cannabinoids reduced viability and induced apoptosis-related programs, with distinct transcriptional changes suggesting engagement of multiple stress-response pathways that could intersect with autophagic flux, mitochondrial quality control, and adaptation to metabolic pressure ref [21], ref [42]. These observations are relevant to therapeutic resistance because tumor cells often exploit autophagy as a survival buffer under drug-induced stress; conversely, excessive or dysregulated autophagy may contribute to cell death when stress exceeds adaptive capacity.

From a precision-oncology perspective, current evidence remains insufficient to define cannabinoid-induced autophagy as uniformly beneficial or harmful across cancers. The available studies support a context-dependent model in which cannabinoid formulations may either sensitize tumors to cytotoxic stress or, in some settings, activate compensatory survival pathways that would require rational combination strategies. Clinically, most oncology-focused human evidence still concerns symptom palliation rather than antitumor efficacy, underscoring the gap between mechanistic preclinical findings and validated therapeutic application ref [52]. Future work should therefore integrate autophagy biomarkers, genomic background, and formulation-specific pharmacology when evaluating cannabinoids as adjuncts in cancer therapy ref [9], ref [21], ref [42], ref [52].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Cancer, Genomic Stability, and Therapeutic Resistance
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Cancer, Genomic Stability, and Therapeutic Resistance - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
An emerging theme in precision oncology is whether cannabinoid-based interventions can modulate autophagy in ways that reshape tumor stress adaptation and treatment response. Broad reviews of cannabis and cancer indicate that cannabinoids influence interconnected programs of apoptosis, mitochondrial dysfunction, ER stress, and autophagy, but the biological outcome is highly context dependent, varying with tumor type, receptor expression, dose, and drug combination strategy ref [40]. This context dependence is especially relevant to autophagy, because the same pathway may constrain early malignant transformation yet later sustain survival under hypoxia, nutrient limitation, and therapeutic pressure.

Preclinical literature summarized in recent cancer-focused reviews suggests that cannabinoids can trigger cytotoxic autophagy or cooperate with apoptosis in some models, while in other settings they may elicit adaptive autophagic flux that buffers metabolic stress and preserves viability ref [40]. Such duality has direct implications for genomic stability and therapeutic resistance: autophagy can limit ROS accumulation and proteotoxic damage, thereby reducing genome-destabilizing stress, but it can also help established cancers tolerate chemotherapy- or radiotherapy-induced injury. Accordingly, combining cannabinoids with standard anticancer agents may be beneficial only when the autophagic response is mechanistically defined and shown to favor tumor cell death rather than survival ref [40].

From a translational perspective, the current clinical literature remains more robust for symptom control than for antitumor efficacy. Reviews of cannabis use in oncology emphasize the stronger evidence base for palliation of pain, nausea, appetite loss, and related treatment burdens, while also noting ongoing interest in next-generation THC-centered formulations and other cannabinoid approaches ref [6], ref [40]. Therefore, any attempt to exploit cannabinoid-regulated autophagy as an anticancer strategy should be framed as hypothesis-driven and biomarker-led, with careful distinction between supportive care benefits and direct effects on tumor progression or resistance biology ref [6], ref [40].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Cancer, Genomic Stability, and Therapeutic Resistance
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Cancer, Genomic Stability, and Therapeutic Resistance - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
From a precision-oncology perspective, therapy-induced autophagy is best viewed as a context-sensitive stress adaptation rather than a uniformly beneficial or harmful process. The broader cannabinoid literature underscores how ligand diversity, receptor bias, and non-canonical signaling can generate markedly different downstream phenotypes, implying that any attempt to exploit autophagy therapeutically in cancer will require careful stratification by compound, receptor engagement, and cellular state rather than simple class-based assumptions ref [36], ref [40]. This logic is reinforced by calls for more rigorous translational prioritization in emerging drug research, where mechanistic heterogeneity is a central barrier to reproducibility and clinical development ref [37].

Several underused lines of evidence are also relevant to resistance biology. THC-linked modulation of dopaminergic circuitry and reward-related neuroadaptations illustrates how chronic exposure can remodel stress-response pathways over time, a principle that may be pertinent when considering sustained cannabinoid-based co-therapies in oncology ref [64], ref [63]. Human studies further show that repeated cannabinoid administration is associated with measurable changes in sleep, withdrawal, and user-reported behavioral responses, emphasizing that host-level tolerability and adaptation could influence adherence to regimens designed to manipulate autophagy during prolonged cancer treatment ref [33], ref [34], ref [39], ref [65].

Methodologically, translation also depends on robust biomarker frameworks. Imaging strategies targeting CB1 receptors provide one route for quantifying target engagement in vivo, while pharmacological analyses of cannabinoid ligands and receptor-directed probes highlight the importance of mapping compound-specific interaction landscapes before linking cannabinoid exposure to autophagy modulation, genomic stress responses, or therapeutic sensitization in tumors ref [66], ref [36], ref [43]. Although immunoregulatory and broad-spectrum cannabinoid effects remain of interest, the current evidence base argues that future studies should integrate receptor pharmacology, longitudinal adaptation, and biomarker-guided patient selection to determine when autophagy inhibition or activation can realistically enhance anti-cancer efficacy ref [38], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Cancer, Genomic Stability, and Therapeutic Resistance
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Cancer, Genomic Stability, and Therapeutic Resistance - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
An emerging translational theme is the intersection between cannabinoid signaling, autophagy, and cancer cell stress adaptation. Broad reviews of cannabis pharmacology and anticancer applications indicate that cannabinoids can influence apoptosis, redox balance, inflammatory signaling, and metabolic programs that converge on autophagic machinery, making autophagy a plausible determinant of whether cannabinoid exposure produces tumor suppression or cytoprotection in malignant cells ref [62], ref [58], ref [30]. This duality is consistent with the broader concept that autophagy can either limit oncogenic damage or support survival under therapeutic stress.

The strongest disease-focused example in the present reference set comes from dermatologic oncology. The review on cannabinoids in inflammatory and neoplastic skin diseases highlights antineoplastic effects relevant to cutaneous tumors, including growth inhibition and pro-death signaling, while also emphasizing the immunologic and microenvironmental complexity of cannabinoid responses ref [67]. In this context, autophagy is mechanistically important because it interfaces with inflammation, organelle quality control, and lysosomal degradation, all of which can reshape tumor fitness and treatment responsiveness. More generally, analyses of cannabis and cancer and of cannabinoid-based biopharmaceutical development argue that the therapeutic value of these agents will depend on tumor subtype, receptor context, and combination strategy rather than on a uniform class effect ref [58], ref [12].

For precision oncology, the key implication is that cannabinoids should be evaluated not only as symptom-control agents but also as modulators of autophagy-linked therapeutic resistance. Preclinical reports in breast and colorectal cancer suggest that distinct cannabinoid preparations can produce divergent antitumor outputs, including apoptosis-related death and altered gene-expression programs, supporting biomarker-guided deployment ref [17], ref [59], ref [60]. Thus, future work should define when cannabinoid-triggered autophagy is cytotoxic versus protective, and whether rational combinations with chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or lysosomal/autophagy inhibitors can convert stress adaptation into durable tumor control ref [62], ref [30], ref [67].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Neurodegenerative, Metabolic, Cardiovascular, and Other Non-Infectious Disorders
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Neurodegenerative, Metabolic, Cardiovascular, and Other Non-Infectious Disorders - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Autophagy is a central homeostatic pathway in non-infectious disease because it coordinates protein turnover, organelle quality control, and metabolic adaptation. Across chronic disorders, defective autophagic flux promotes accumulation of damaged mitochondria and misfolded substrates, whereas excessive or maladaptive activation can also contribute to tissue injury, underscoring its context-dependent, "double-edged" character ref [3], ref [12]. This balance is especially relevant in long-lived cells and metabolically active tissues, where basal autophagy sustains cellular fitness under nutrient fluctuation and stress ref [11], ref [12].

In metabolic disease, autophagy intersects directly with lipid and glucose handling. Lipophagy mobilizes intracellular lipid droplets and links lysosomal degradation to systemic energy homeostasis; its dysregulation contributes to steatosis, insulin resistance, and broader metabolic dysfunction ref [68], ref [12]. More generally, nutrient-sensing networks that regulate autophagy also shape tumor-associated energy metabolism, highlighting how the same pathway may preserve survival in one setting yet facilitate pathology in another ref [3], ref [12].

Comparable principles apply in degenerative and cardiovascular disorders. In the heart, cardiomyocyte autophagy helps cells adapt to metabolic stress, remove dysfunctional organelles, and preserve contractile competence, whereas impaired regulation may favor energetic failure and remodeling ref [11]. In neurodegenerative and ocular disease, selective autophagy receptors such as optineurin are particularly important for cargo recognition, and disease-associated mutations can compromise proteostasis and mitochondrial clearance, as illustrated in glaucoma and related disorders ref [16]. Mitochondrial damage is also a potent trigger of sterile inflammation, linking defective mitophagy to autoinflammatory signaling ref [18]. At the lysosomal end of the pathway, storage disorders further demonstrate that failed substrate clearance can drive multisystem degeneration and motivate therapies aimed at restoring lysosomal-autophagic function ref [21].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Neurodegenerative, Metabolic, Cardiovascular, and Other Non-Infectious Disorders
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Neurodegenerative, Metabolic, Cardiovascular, and Other Non-Infectious Disorders - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
An important cross-cutting theme in non-infectious disease is the intersection between endocannabinoid signaling and autophagy, particularly in the nervous system. Broad reviews of cannabis–brain interactions show that cannabinoid-responsive pathways regulate synaptic activity, mitochondrial function, stress signaling, and neuroinflammatory tone, all of which are major upstream determinants of autophagic flux in neurons and glia ref [34]. Structure–activity analyses of cannabis-derived compounds further indicate that chemically distinct cannabinoids can differentially engage neuronal survival and excitability pathways, supporting the idea that autophagy-relevant outcomes are highly ligand- and context-dependent rather than uniform class effects ref [49].

This interface is also relevant to metabolic and degenerative disease. The reported association between cannabis exposure and lower body mass index has been interpreted in light of altered energy balance and nutrient sensing, processes tightly coupled to autophagy regulation through AMPK–mTOR-related networks ref [16]. In parallel, anti-inflammatory actions of cannabinoids documented in dermatomyositis models, including suppression of TNF-α and type I interferon responses, are mechanistically pertinent because chronic cytokine signaling can disrupt autophagic homeostasis and amplify tissue injury ref [54]. Thus, cannabinoid-dependent immunometabolic reprogramming may indirectly reshape autophagy in inflammatory myopathies and related systemic disorders.

A similar framework extends to musculoskeletal and other chronic degenerative conditions. Detection of cannabinoid receptors in osteoarthritic cartilage suggests that chondrocytes are positioned to respond to cannabinoid ligands in ways potentially relevant to autophagy-mediated matrix turnover, inflammatory restraint, and cellular survival under mechanical stress ref [58]. Collectively, these observations support the view that cannabinoid-responsive networks should be considered modulators of autophagy-linked proteostasis, organelle quality control, and inflammatory adaptation across neurodegenerative, metabolic, and degenerative diseases, while also underscoring the need for disease-specific mechanistic studies before therapeutic translation ref [34], ref [49], ref [54], ref [58].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Neurodegenerative, Metabolic, Cardiovascular, and Other Non-Infectious Disorders
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Neurodegenerative, Metabolic, Cardiovascular, and Other Non-Infectious Disorders - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
In non-infectious disorders, the intersection between autophagy and endocannabinoid signaling is increasingly relevant because both systems regulate cellular stress adaptation, mitochondrial function, inflammatory tone, and metabolic homeostasis. Broad reviews of the endocannabinoid system in the brain and peripheral tissues indicate that cannabinoid-responsive pathways influence neuronal excitability, glial activation, energy balance, and survival programs that are mechanistically linked to autophagic flux, lysosomal turnover, and organelle quality control ref [24], ref [35]. This conceptual overlap is particularly important in chronic degenerative conditions, where insufficient clearance of damaged proteins or organelles amplifies tissue dysfunction.

Neurological diseases provide a prominent example. In the central nervous system, endocannabinoid signaling has been implicated in neuroprotection, synaptic regulation, and modulation of neuroinflammation, all of which can shape autophagy-dependent maintenance of proteostasis and neuronal integrity ref [24]. Clinical imaging work in multiple sclerosis further suggests that cannabis use is associated with altered cerebral metabolism and disability-related parameters, consistent with disease-modifying effects on stress and inflammatory pathways that may converge on autophagy-regulated homeostasis ref [31]. Related clinical hypotheses such as endocannabinoid deficiency in migraine, fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, and other treatment-resistant syndromes also point to a broader homeostatic role for this signaling axis in disorders characterized by persistent stress, pain, and dysregulated inflammatory responses ref [37].

Metabolic and degenerative disorders show similar convergence. Cannabinoid-based approaches have been discussed for type 2 diabetes, where nutrient sensing, lipid handling, insulin responsiveness, and inflammation are tightly connected to autophagic control of cellular metabolism ref [56]. In ocular disease, Cannabis sativa extracts have been explored for retinopathy, a condition in which oxidative stress, vascular injury, and defective cellular clearance contribute to tissue damage ref [49]. Beyond neural and metabolic tissues, cannabidiol has been shown to enhance fracture healing and stimulate lysyl hydroxylase activity in osteoblasts, highlighting potential interactions with matrix remodeling and quality-control pathways relevant to skeletal degeneration and repair ref [20]. Collectively, these observations support the view that cannabinoid-endocannabinoid signaling may complement autophagy-centered strategies across neurodegenerative, metabolic, retinal, and musculoskeletal disorders, although direct mechanistic and translational evidence remains incomplete ref [35], ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Neurodegenerative, Metabolic, Cardiovascular, and Other Non-Infectious Disorders
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Neurodegenerative, Metabolic, Cardiovascular, and Other Non-Infectious Disorders - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A useful extension of autophagy-centered discussion in non-infectious disease is the endocannabinoid system, which intersects with nutrient sensing, neuronal excitability, pain processing, and psychiatric homeostasis. In metabolic regulation, endocannabinoid signaling is a recognized modulator of food intake and energy balance, linking CB1-dependent hypothalamic and peripheral pathways to feeding behavior and adiposity; because autophagy is likewise tightly integrated with AMPK–mTOR signaling and cellular fuel availability, these systems likely converge in disorders characterized by altered lipid handling and metabolic stress ref [18].

In neurological disease, cannabinoid-based interventions have been explored in epilepsy, seizure-associated neuroprotection, chronic pain, and multiple sclerosis-related symptoms, all settings in which defective autophagy, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuroinflammation are prominent pathogenic themes. Preclinical evidence indicates anticonvulsant and neuroprotective actions of cannabinoids in animal seizure models ref [26], while broader neurological pharmacology reviews describe their relevance across spasticity, pain, and other CNS disorders ref [40]. Clinically, analgesic benefit has been most consistently discussed for neuropathic pain and multiple-sclerosis-associated pain, including meta-analytic support, although effect sizes and tolerability remain variable ref [21], ref [37].

At the same time, neuropsychiatric outcomes caution against simplistic therapeutic extrapolation. Integrative analyses of cannabis and schizophrenia indicate that cannabinoid exposure can aggravate psychosis-related vulnerability in susceptible populations ref [48]. Thus, in the context of autophagy-oriented therapy for neurodegenerative and other chronic disorders, cannabinoid signaling should be viewed as a pleiotropic modifier rather than a uniformly protective axis: it may alleviate excitotoxicity, pain, or metabolic imbalance in some settings, yet worsen cognitive or psychiatric trajectories in others ref [40], ref [48].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Neurodegenerative, Metabolic, Cardiovascular, and Other Non-Infectious Disorders
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Neurodegenerative, Metabolic, Cardiovascular, and Other Non-Infectious Disorders - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A relevant extension of autophagy research in non-infectious disorders concerns the endocannabinoid system, which intersects with neuronal survival, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial homeostasis, and lysosomal trafficking. Broad overviews of endocannabinoid signaling in nervous system health indicate that cannabinoid pathways influence glial activation, oxidative stress responses, and synaptic resilience, all of which converge functionally with autophagy-dependent quality control mechanisms in chronic neurodegeneration ref [56]. More generally, cannabinoid receptor biology has expanded beyond neurotransmission alone, with CB2-centered signaling increasingly linked to immune modulation and tissue-protective responses that may indirectly favor restoration of autophagic balance under disease conditions ref [24], ref [40].

This interface is especially pertinent in movement disorders. Reviews of Parkinson’s disease and related hyperkinetic or hypokinetic syndromes suggest that cannabinoids may attenuate excitotoxicity, neuroinflammation, and abnormal circuit activity, while also influencing pathways relevant to proteostasis and damaged-organelle clearance, making them conceptually compatible with autophagy-targeted neuroprotection strategies ref [15], ref [30], ref [56]. In parallel, microglial studies showing that cannabidiol alters circadian clock-core regulatory networks are notable because circadian disruption is increasingly recognized as a modifier of autophagic flux, inflammatory tone, and neurodegenerative progression ref [57].

In demyelinating and inflammatory neurological disease, cannabinoid-based interventions have mainly been evaluated for symptom relief, yet their broader biological effects are also relevant to autophagy-centered models of tissue homeostasis. Clinical and translational discussions in multiple sclerosis emphasize immunomodulation, spasticity control, and neuroprotection ref [59], while wider analyses of cannabinoid pharmacology in inflammatory disorders support the idea that dampening maladaptive immune activation could secondarily preserve autophagy-dependent cellular housekeeping in the CNS and peripheral tissues ref [40], ref [24]. Overall, although direct mechanistic evidence remains incomplete, the cannabinoid-autophagy axis represents a plausible therapeutic bridge across neurodegenerative and other chronic non-infectious diseases ref [56], ref [30], ref [59].

subsections.section_title: Lifestyle, Environmental, and Behavioral Determinants of Autophagy in Disease Risk and Prevention
subsections.subsection_title: Lifestyle, Environmental, and Behavioral Determinants of Autophagy in Disease Risk and Prevention - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A central lifestyle determinant of autophagy is systemic energy balance. Nutrient scarcity, exercise, and intermittent metabolic stress generally activate autophagic programs through AMPK and reciprocal inhibition of mTOR, thereby promoting cellular housekeeping, mitochondrial quality control, and adaptation to fluctuating substrate availability ref [5], ref [12]. This metabolic wiring is especially relevant to prevention, because impaired autophagic flux contributes to obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and other chronic metabolic disorders, whereas appropriately induced autophagy supports resilience under physiological stress ref [12]. The context dependence of this response is important: autophagy can preserve homeostasis in normal tissues yet also sustain survival of stressed premalignant or malignant cells, underscoring its dual role in disease risk across the lifespan ref [2].

Dietary patterns also shape selective forms of autophagy involved in fuel handling. Lipid overload and defective autophagic lipolysis disturb lipid droplet turnover, favor ectopic fat accumulation, and worsen metabolic inflexibility, linking everyday nutritional excess to hepatic and systemic disease risk ref [6], ref [12]. Conversely, cardiometabolic tissues appear to benefit from tightly regulated autophagy during shifts in substrate use. In the heart, AMPK-driven autophagic responses help maintain ATP balance during ischemic or nutrient-limited conditions, while chronic dysregulation can contribute to pathology if excessive or insufficient ref [5], ref [11]. Thus, exercise and dietary moderation are best viewed not merely as behavioral recommendations, but as upstream modulators of organ-specific autophagic set points.

Age modifies these lifestyle effects. Basal autophagic efficiency declines with aging, reducing the capacity to clear damaged proteins, lipids, and organelles and increasing susceptibility to chronic inflammatory, pulmonary, and cardiovascular disorders ref [25], ref [11]. This age-related loss of proteostatic reserve means that the same environmental exposures—overnutrition, inactivity, or recurrent ischemic stress—may produce greater pathological consequences in older adults than in younger individuals ref [25], ref [12]. Accordingly, preventive strategies that restore physiologic autophagy through sustained physical activity, improved metabolic control, and avoidance of chronic nutrient excess may have broad relevance for reducing both non-communicable disease burden and vulnerability to stress-related tissue injury ref [5], ref [6], ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Lifestyle, Environmental, and Behavioral Determinants of Autophagy in Disease Risk and Prevention
subsections.subsection_title: Lifestyle, Environmental, and Behavioral Determinants of Autophagy in Disease Risk and Prevention - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Cannabis exposure is an increasingly relevant behavioral determinant of autophagy because it intersects with metabolism, neuroadaptation, pulmonary biology, and immune regulation. From a preventive-health perspective, the major issue is not simply cannabinoid pharmacology, but how chronicity, age at exposure, route of administration, and co-use with other substances reshape endocannabinoid signaling that normally helps coordinate cellular stress responses. Adolescent exposure is of particular concern because it occurs during active neurodevelopment and has been associated with persistent behavioral and neurobiological consequences, implying a life-course window in which autophagy-linked homeostatic programs may be especially vulnerable to dysregulation ref [69].

Repeated cannabis use produces tolerance and withdrawal, indicating sustained receptor-level and circuit-level adaptation rather than transient exposure effects ref [12], ref [36]. In humans, chronic heavy cannabis use downregulates brain CB1 receptors, with implications for nutrient sensing, mitochondrial function, and lysosomal turnover pathways that are closely coupled to autophagic balance ref [47]. These adaptations are also relevant to body-weight regulation: epidemiologic observations of lower BMI in some cannabis users have prompted mechanistic models centered on altered energy intake, peripheral metabolism, and endocannabinoid tone, all of which are conceptually linked to lipophagy and metabolic autophagy ref [16]. Thus, cannabis use may influence disease susceptibility through both direct tissue effects and broader remodeling of stress-response networks.

Route of exposure further modifies risk. Cannabis vaping and other e-cigarette-based delivery systems increase access, frequency, and product heterogeneity, potentially changing pulmonary toxicant burden and systemic biological responses ref [59]. In the lung, cannabis, cannabinoids, and endocannabinoids affect airway inflammation, epithelial function, and host defense, processes in which autophagy can either preserve barrier integrity or contribute to maladaptive remodeling depending on context ref [60]. Moreover, alcohol-cannabis interactions converge on CB1 signaling in reward and behavioral regulation, suggesting that polysubstance use may amplify disturbances in cellular stress handling and thereby alter vulnerability to both infectious and non-communicable disease ref [45]. Overall, these data support treating cannabis exposure as a modifiable lifestyle factor with age-, dose-, and route-dependent implications for autophagy-informed disease prevention ref [69], ref [12], ref [36], ref [47], ref [59], ref [60].

subsections.section_title: Lifestyle, Environmental, and Behavioral Determinants of Autophagy in Disease Risk and Prevention
subsections.subsection_title: Lifestyle, Environmental, and Behavioral Determinants of Autophagy in Disease Risk and Prevention - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Cannabis exposure is an increasingly relevant behavioral determinant of autophagy because the endocannabinoid system coordinates neuronal activity, appetite, energy balance, stress responses, and immune signaling—processes that converge on canonical autophagy regulators such as mTOR and AMPK. Broad reviews of cannabinoid biology indicate that CB1- and CB2-centered signaling is highly context dependent, varying with ligand, dose, tissue, and exposure pattern, which helps explain why cannabis-related effects may be either adaptive or maladaptive for disease risk across the lifespan ref [24], ref [25]. In the brain in particular, endocannabinoid signaling links environmental stimuli to synaptic and metabolic homeostasis, suggesting a plausible mechanistic route by which repeated cannabis use could reshape autophagy-dependent proteostasis, mitochondrial quality control, and neuroinflammatory tone ref [24].

From a prevention perspective, the major concern is not simply cannabinoid receptor activation, but the interaction between route of administration, chronicity, and host metabolic state. Population-level evidence associating cannabis smoking with altered C-reactive protein distributions supports the view that inhalational use can modify systemic inflammatory set points ref [39]. At the same time, interest in cannabinoids for metabolic disorders, including type 2 diabetes, reflects their capacity to influence lipid handling, insulin sensitivity, and adipose-endocrine crosstalk—pathways tightly interwoven with autophagic flux ref [56]. Cannabidiol has attracted special attention because it lacks classic intoxicating effects and has been discussed as a candidate modulator in multiple medical settings; however, reviews emphasize that its clinical actions remain heterogeneous and formulation dependent ref [35], ref [52].

These complexities are important for public health messaging. Safety reviews note that cannabidiol can produce adverse effects and drug interactions, arguing against the assumption that all cannabis-derived products are intrinsically benign ref [52]. Likewise, cannabis hyperemesis syndrome illustrates how chronic exposure may convert a behavior perceived as therapeutic into a disorder marked by recurrent gastrointestinal dysfunction and health-care utilization ref [60]. Thus, cannabis-related behaviors should be framed within autophagy-informed precision prevention: low-confidence claims of benefit should be separated from evidence-based contexts, and future work should clarify when cannabinoid signaling supports resilience versus when it aggravates inflammatory, metabolic, neurologic, or gastrointestinal vulnerability ref [25], ref [35], ref [56], ref [60].

subsections.section_title: Lifestyle, Environmental, and Behavioral Determinants of Autophagy in Disease Risk and Prevention
subsections.subsection_title: Lifestyle, Environmental, and Behavioral Determinants of Autophagy in Disease Risk and Prevention - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Cannabis exposure and endocannabinoid tone represent behavior-linked modulators of autophagy with implications for disease susceptibility. Historically, cannabinoid pharmacology has evolved from plant-derived Δ9-THC to endogenous ligands such as anandamide, revealing a signaling network that regulates neuronal activity, metabolism, and stress adaptation through CB1- and CB2-dependent pathways ref [51], ref [81], ref [39]. Because autophagy is tightly coupled to nutrient sensing and intracellular quality control, lifestyle patterns that alter cannabinoid signaling may secondarily influence autophagic flux, particularly in brain, immune, and metabolic tissues.

A major preventive-health context is energy balance. The endogenous cannabinoid system is a recognized modulator of appetite and food intake, linking hedonic feeding behavior to peripheral metabolic control ref [18]. CB1 signaling is therefore relevant to obesogenic lifestyles, in which chronic nutrient excess generally suppresses protective autophagy and favors lipid accumulation, insulin resistance, and inflammatory stress. Conversely, broad reviews of cannabis and cannabinoids indicate that exogenous cannabinoid exposure can variably affect feeding, body weight regulation, and systemic physiology depending on dose, composition, and route of administration ref [22], ref [81]. Cannabidiol is of particular interest because, unlike THC, it has a wide spectrum of pharmacological actions with comparatively distinct psychoactive liabilities, making it a candidate for disentangling beneficial metabolic or cytoprotective signaling from maladaptive behavioral effects ref [38].

These interactions are also relevant to host defense and developmental programming. Cannabinoid-induced apoptosis in immune cells provides one mechanistic basis for immunosuppression, suggesting that sustained or inappropriate cannabinoid exposure could weaken antimicrobial responses even if it alleviates inflammation in some settings ref [105]. At the same time, detection of CB1 receptors and FAAH in the human placenta underscores that endocannabinoid signaling operates at the maternal-fetal interface, raising concern that prenatal environmental exposures affecting this system may influence developmental homeostasis, possibly including autophagy-related processes ref [42]. Overall, cannabinoid-associated behaviors should be viewed as double-edged determinants of autophagy-linked risk: potentially useful for symptom control and metabolic modulation, yet capable of promoting immune vulnerability or developmental perturbation when exposure patterns are unfavorable ref [22], ref [51].

subsections.section_title: Lifestyle, Environmental, and Behavioral Determinants of Autophagy in Disease Risk and Prevention
subsections.subsection_title: Lifestyle, Environmental, and Behavioral Determinants of Autophagy in Disease Risk and Prevention - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
The endocannabinoid system is a plausible lifestyle-responsive regulator linking feeding behavior, gut physiology, stress adaptation, and neuroimmune tone to autophagy-dependent disease risk. As a broadly distributed lipid signaling network, it integrates nutritional state and reward circuitry with peripheral metabolic and inflammatory responses, thereby positioning cannabinoid signaling at the interface between behavioral exposures and cellular quality-control programs ref [41], ref [10]. This framework is especially relevant to prevention research because autophagy is highly sensitive to energy balance, circadian timing, and inflammatory burden, all of which are influenced by endocannabinoid tone.

Dietary pattern and obesity are particularly important determinants. Endocannabinoid signaling in the gut contributes to appetite regulation, intestinal permeability, host–microbe interactions, and nutrient handling, suggesting one route by which lifestyle-associated metabolic stress may reshape autophagy in barrier tissues and liver–adipose axes ref [109], ref [41]. Reviews of targeted modulators further indicate that pharmacologic or behavioral attenuation of excessive endocannabinoid signaling could have utility in obesity and addiction-related phenotypes, both of which are tightly linked to chronic autophagy dysregulation and cardiometabolic disease risk ref [23], ref [10].

Behavioral stressors and substance-use patterns add a second layer. Endocannabinoid modulation influences cognitive and emotional behavior, reward processing, and dependence mechanisms, indicating that stress exposure, compulsive intake, and maladaptive reinforcement may alter autophagy indirectly through neuroendocrine and inflammatory pathways ref [38], ref [50]. Cannabinoid signaling also shapes immune-cell activity and inflammatory responses, with implications for autophagy-mediated host defense and chronic inflammatory disease susceptibility ref [40]. Finally, circadian disruption appears relevant: cannabidiol can modify core clock regulation in microglia, supporting the concept that sleep–wake behavior and circadian hygiene may intersect with cannabinoid-autophagy crosstalk in neuroinflammatory prevention strategies ref [57].

subsections.section_title: Translational and Therapeutic Frontiers: Drug Discovery, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Translational and Therapeutic Frontiers: Drug Discovery, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A central translational priority in autophagy research is the shift from broad pathway activation or inhibition toward mechanism-informed drug discovery. Because autophagy can suppress early tumorigenesis yet support survival of established cancers under metabolic stress, therapeutic design must account for disease stage, tissue context, and energetic state rather than treating autophagy as uniformly beneficial or harmful ref [2]. This same context dependence is evident in metabolic disease and cardiovascular injury, where AMPK-linked autophagic responses may preserve homeostasis, but excessive or prolonged activation can become maladaptive ref [5], ref [11], ref [12].

Current drug discovery efforts therefore increasingly focus on actionable nodes upstream and downstream of the core machinery, including nutrient sensing, lysosomal competence, mitochondrial quality control, and cargo selectivity. Reviews of lysosomal storage disorders illustrate how defective lysosome-dependent flux can itself be a therapeutic target, motivating strategies that combine substrate reduction, enzyme restoration, and enhancement of autophagic clearance ref [21]. In inflammatory settings, mitochondrial dysfunction and danger signaling further position mitophagy and mitochondrial surveillance as promising translational targets, especially where autoinflammation is driven by unresolved organelle stress ref [18].

Future clinical application will depend on better patient stratification and pharmacodynamic monitoring. The intersection of autophagy with ubiquitination and DNA repair highlights why combination regimens may outperform monotherapy, particularly in oncology where stress adaptation and genome maintenance shape treatment response ref [9]. Interest in unconventional modulators, including cannabinoid-based agents in cancer, also underscores the need to determine whether observed antitumor effects involve productive autophagic flux, cytoprotective recycling, or autophagy-associated cell death before advancing such compounds into precision trials ref [57], ref [2].

Taken together, the translational frontier is moving toward disease-specific, flux-aware, and combination-based intervention frameworks. Progress will require biomarkers that distinguish autophagy induction from completion, and trial designs that integrate metabolic status, mitochondrial injury, and lysosomal function into therapeutic decision making ref [11], ref [12], ref [18], ref [21].

subsections.section_title: Translational and Therapeutic Frontiers: Drug Discovery, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Translational and Therapeutic Frontiers: Drug Discovery, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A major translational frontier in autophagy-linked therapeutics is the standardization of complex natural-product platforms, particularly cannabinoid-based medicines. From a drug-discovery perspective, recent biopharmaceutical analyses emphasize that progress depends on moving beyond heterogeneous plant extracts toward reproducible, mechanism-informed formulations with defined composition, pharmacokinetics, and manufacturing quality, all of which are prerequisites for evaluating whether cannabinoids can modulate autophagy in clinically useful ways ref [113], ref [32], ref [57]. This is especially important because enthusiasm for medical cannabis frequently exceeds the strength of evidence, creating a gap between preclinical promise and evidence-based deployment ref [57], ref [32].

Production technologies are therefore becoming central to therapeutic translation. Engineering yeasts as biosynthetic platforms offers a scalable route to rare or customized cannabinoids, facilitating medicinal chemistry, structure-function studies, and the generation of compounds better suited for selective pathway interrogation, including autophagy-related signaling ref [31]. In parallel, plant in vitro culture systems provide controlled alternatives to field cultivation, enabling metabolite consistency and potentially reducing batch variability that complicates preclinical and clinical interpretation ref [56]. Together, these manufacturing innovations support a shift from empirical cannabis use toward pharmaceutical-grade libraries and formulations ref [113], ref [31], ref [56].

Clinically, the next step is not simply broader adoption but smarter trial design. Reviews of cannabis research and evidence-based medical use consistently argue for indication-specific studies, rigorous dose standardization, adverse-effect surveillance, and regulatory frameworks aligned with conventional drug development ref [32], ref [57]. For autophagy-centered applications, this implies integrating biomarker strategies, distinguishing whole-plant from single-molecule interventions, and prioritizing patient subsets in which cannabinoid-responsive stress, inflammatory, or metabolic pathways are mechanistically relevant ref [113], ref [57]. Thus, the future lies in converging autophagy biology, biomanufacturing, and evidence-based cannabinoid therapeutics rather than treating cannabis products as intrinsically translatable medicines ref [31], ref [32], ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Translational and Therapeutic Frontiers: Drug Discovery, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Translational and Therapeutic Frontiers: Drug Discovery, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A major translational frontier is the repositioning of cannabinoid and endocannabinoid modulators as adjuncts to autophagy-targeted therapy, particularly where inflammation, pain, metabolic dysregulation, and treatment resistance intersect. Broad pharmacological reviews indicate that phytocannabinoids and endocannabinoid-system modulators influence multiple signaling hubs relevant to autophagic control, while also offering tractable medicinal-chemistry entry points for multi-target drug design ref [17], ref [35]. This is especially attractive for complex disorders in which symptom relief and disease modification may need to be pursued simultaneously.

Clinically, the most mature opportunities lie in symptom-directed applications that could later be linked to mechanism-based stratification. Evidence for analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antiemetic activity supports cannabinoids as candidates for integrated supportive care, including chronic pain states where autophagy and neuroimmune signaling are increasingly implicated ref [43], ref [54]. The concept of clinical endocannabinoid deficiency further suggests that subsets of patients with migraine, fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, and related treatment-refractory syndromes may benefit from precision approaches based on endocannabinoid tone rather than one-size-fits-all prescribing ref [37]. In metabolic disease, cannabinoid-based interventions have also been discussed for type 2 diabetes, although efficacy, receptor selectivity, and off-target liabilities remain important barriers to routine translation ref [56], ref [17].

Future progress will depend on balancing therapeutic promise with formulation, dosing, and safety challenges. Cannabidiol has attracted particular attention because of its broad therapeutic window and non-intoxicating profile, yet reviews of clinical and preclinical data emphasize adverse effects, drug-drug interactions, and product-quality variability that complicate regulatory approval and long-term use ref [52], ref [35]. Accordingly, next-generation development should prioritize standardized preparations, biomarker-guided trials, and mechanistic endpoints that clarify when cannabinoid interventions truly modulate disease-relevant pathways, including autophagy, rather than merely providing symptomatic benefit ref [17], ref [54], ref [52].

subsections.section_title: Translational and Therapeutic Frontiers: Drug Discovery, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Translational and Therapeutic Frontiers: Drug Discovery, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A major translational frontier is the development of cannabinoid-based analgesic and neurologic therapies that could modulate autophagy-linked stress, inflammation, and cell-survival pathways while reducing reliance on conventional sedative or opioid-centered regimens. Clinical interest is strongest in chronic pain, neuropathic pain, multiple sclerosis-related symptoms, and selected neurologic disorders, where the cannabinoid system offers a mechanistically distinct target with both central and peripheral actions ref [21], ref [47], ref [40]. Meta-analytic and review-level evidence suggests modest but clinically meaningful benefit in some refractory pain states, although effect sizes vary with formulation, dose, and study quality ref [37], ref [47].

From a drug-discovery perspective, current strategies increasingly favor defined formulations over crude preparations. Oromucosal combination products containing tetrahydrocannabinol/cannabidiol exemplify this shift, aiming to improve pharmacokinetic predictability and tolerability while preserving multimodal efficacy ref [50], ref [40]. Parallel efforts seek non-psychoactive or low-psychoactivity analogs such as ajulemic acid, which may retain analgesic and anti-inflammatory properties without a pronounced "high," thereby widening the therapeutic window for chronic use ref [44], ref [47]. Cannabidiol itself remains attractive because of its broad pharmacology and relative lack of intoxication, making it a candidate scaffold for combination therapy and precision reformulation ref [82], ref [40].

However, translation remains constrained by unresolved safety and biological complexity. Cannabinoid-mediated immunosuppressive effects, including apoptosis in immune cells, may be therapeutically useful in inflammatory settings but raise concerns in infection-prone or immunocompromised patients ref [118]. Future trials therefore need biomarker-guided patient stratification, standardized chemotypes, and endpoints that integrate analgesia, neurologic function, immune effects, and autophagy-relevant disease activity. Such design principles will be essential for determining whether cannabinoid medicines can move from symptomatic adjuncts to mechanism-informed interventions in chronic inflammatory and neurodegenerative disease ref [21], ref [50], ref [82].

subsections.section_title: Translational and Therapeutic Frontiers: Drug Discovery, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Translational and Therapeutic Frontiers: Drug Discovery, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A major future direction in autophagy-linked therapeutics is the rational integration of cannabinoid pharmacology with precision modulation of inflammatory, metabolic, and neuroimmune pathways. The endocannabinoid system is attractive translationally because it offers multiple intervention nodes—CB1, CB2, ligand synthesis and degradation, and biased or allosteric signaling—rather than a single receptor-centric strategy, creating opportunities to tune autophagy indirectly while limiting psychotropic liability ref [10], ref [21], ref [23]. In this framework, CB2-focused approaches are especially compelling because of their immunoregulatory profile and more favorable central adverse-effect expectations, making them plausible candidates for chronic inflammatory and infection-associated disorders in which autophagy and immune homeostasis intersect ref [24], ref [40].

Clinically, however, enthusiasm must be balanced by the uneven maturity of the evidence base. Reviews of therapeutic cannabinoid use indicate that approved or near-clinic formulations have mainly advanced in symptom control rather than mechanism-driven disease modification, while substantial heterogeneity persists across indications, formulations, and dosing paradigms ref [18], ref [10]. Safety also remains a translational bottleneck: systematic assessment of medical cannabinoids documents adverse neuropsychiatric, gastrointestinal, and cardiovascular effects that are highly relevant when long-term autophagy modulation is envisioned for prevention or chronic therapy ref [13]. These realities argue for biomarker-guided trials that distinguish target engagement, autophagic flux effects, and symptomatic benefit rather than treating all cannabinoid interventions as pharmacologically equivalent ref [21], ref [24].

Future progress will also depend on regulatory clarity and compound standardization. The evolving U.S. status of cannabidiol illustrates how commercial availability can outpace mechanistic validation, manufacturing consistency, and evidence-based labeling, complicating trial design and comparative effectiveness assessment ref [90]. Accordingly, next-generation development is shifting toward targeted modulators of the endogenous cannabinoid system, including receptor-selective agonists/antagonists and enzyme-directed strategies for addiction, obesity, and inflammatory disease, where autophagy may serve as both a mechanistic biomarker and a therapeutic co-target ref [23], ref [21], ref [40]. Overall, the field is moving from broad cannabinoid exposure toward receptor-, pathway-, and context-specific intervention—an essential step for converting autophagy–cannabinoid biology into reliable preventive and therapeutic medicine ref [18], ref [24].
